When you describe someone as haggard, you mean they look extremely exhausted, worn out, and unwell — and it shows clearly on their face.

Haggard is a word used to describe a person's appearance, almost always their face or overall look. A haggard person doesn't just look a little tired — they look like they have been through something hard. Their face looks strained, thin, and drained of life. Think of sunken eyes, hollow or drawn cheeks, a pale complexion, and deep lines of stress or fatigue. It is the look of someone who has been suffering for a while.

This is an important point: haggard is not the word you use when someone looks slightly sleepy after one bad night. It describes a more serious, visible deterioration — the kind that happens after days of no sleep, prolonged worry, serious illness, grief, or relentless overwork. There is a sense that time and hardship have taken a toll on the person, and their face is showing it.

Someone might look haggard because of:

  • Chronic lack of sleep or exhaustion
  • Long-term stress or anxiety
  • A serious or prolonged illness
  • Deep grief or emotional suffering
  • Starvation or physical deprivation

The common thread is that something has been wearing the person down, and their face has started to show the damage.

When you call someone haggard, the tone is usually sympathetic or observational — not cruel. You are noticing that this person looks like they are struggling. A doctor might look at a patient and say they look haggard. A friend who hasn't slept in three days might be described as haggard. The word carries a sense of concern or pity, not mockery.
How it differs from similar words

Several words come close to haggard, but each one has a slightly different focus:

Tired or sleepy just means low on energy. You can feel tired and still look fine. Haggard means the exhaustion is so deep and lasting that it is visible on your face and body.

Gaunt focuses specifically on looking dangerously thin, almost skeletal. A haggard person may or may not be thin — what matters is the overall look of suffering and fatigue.

Weary describes how someone feels — heavy, drained, and lacking motivation. Haggard describes how someone looks.

Drawn is the closest relative to haggard. A drawn face looks tight, strained, and thin from stress. Haggard is slightly stronger and broader — it includes the exhaustion, the pallor, the hollow eyes, the whole picture.

So if tired is a 3 out of 10 on the exhaustion scale, haggard is closer to an 8 or 9 — and crucially, it is always about visible appearance, not just an internal feeling.
How it is used in sentences

Here are natural examples showing how the word works in practice:

  • "After three sleepless nights with a sick child, she looked haggard and pale."
  • "The soldiers returned from the battlefield with haggard faces and distant eyes."
  • "He had lost weight and looked haggard from months of caring for his ailing father."
  • "The detective investigating the case appeared haggard — clearly, he hadn't been home in days."
  • "Her haggard expression told me she had been crying all night."

Notice that the word is almost always paired with something related to the face or appearance: haggard face, haggard look, haggard expression, haggard eyes, looked haggard. That's its natural home.

Haggard is a moderately formal word. You would find it comfortably in a novel, a news article, or careful conversation. It's not slang, and it's not stiff academic language either. It sits right in the middle — educated, clear, and expressive.

Haggard means looking visibly exhausted, worn out, and unwell — especially on the face — as a result of prolonged stress, illness, grief, or lack of sleep.

If you remember that image — a face that looks like it has been through something hard and is showing every bit of it — you will never misuse this word.
